text: I'm Ted Sides, and this is Capital Allocators.
My guest on today's show is Stephen MacLennan, the Co-Chief Investment Officer of the Ontario
Teachers Pension Plan, where he oversees asset allocation for the $300 billion fund responsible

Please enjoy my conversation with Steven McLennan.
Steven, thanks so much for joining me.
Thanks for having me, Ted, big fan of the podcast.
I'd love you to take me back to the early experiences that later you could look back
and say influenced your investing.
I'm not sure what it was. It was probably something related to the pop culture in the 80s,
the movies, and the TV shows of the time. My first foray into the investing world was
when my last year of high school, I did a co-op session at one of the local brokerage firms.
It coincided with the first Gulf War. As tragic as those circumstances were for the people on
the ground, the connection between what was happening in the real world in terms of what
was going on in CNN, how that transmitted immediately into what was going on in the
markets. You could see that real-time reaction. That was the start of how I started to think about
the investing world. I've done a number of different things career-wise. Each of those
experiences has shaped me in terms of how I think about the world.
What were some of those experiences and how did they shape your views?
Coming out of high school, I did an undergraduate degree in business and economics and finance.
My first job out of school was working for Archer Daniels Midland, which is the big U.S.
agribusiness company for the Canadian operations. It involved buying and selling grain and involved
logistics and involved hedging on the Chicago exchange. It was an interesting foray into the
business world. It wasn't necessarily a pure investment type of role. The plan was always
to go back to school to do my MBA. After my MBA, I ended up joining Merrill Lynch in their
Calgary office. Calgary is the energy hub of Canada, the Houston of Canada. It's a capital
intensive sector. There was a lot of capital raising required as part of that job. Merrill
was well positioned to do that. Combined with a lot of activity from U.S. companies coming in,
buying some of the Canadian E&P entities, I got exposure to that. For personal reasons,
my now wife wanted to move back to Toronto to go back to school and to be closer to family.
I used that as an opportunity to think about what is the next stage of my career?
How do I want to position myself to get closer to the investment process? Move away from that
agent type of role as an investment banker to more of a principal type of role as an investor.
Use that to go back to school. Did a mathematical finance degree here in Toronto.
Then I joined teachers as a new entrant junior person. I joined the credit desk. Given my
background, it was a wide mandate at the time. This would have been 2003. The credit business
would have been your traditional corporate bonds, some private placements. Credit derivatives was
a growing business. That was where I spent the bulk of my time thinking about how best to use
that product to implement whatever views we thought were appropriate at the time. The GFC was a
credit derivative event. Lots of scars on my back from that particular experience. How do you deal
with liquidity, counterparties, risk positioning, blocking and tackling portfolio construction
was eventually elevated to be leading the credit team. It was a fantastic team.
In 2013, the head of our capital markets group had been tasked with building a new program called
Natural Resources, which was a combination of our public commodity program, which we use for
its inflation characteristics, combined with an aspiration to grow a private natural resource
program to be a complement to those public commodities exposures. It was a great opportunity
for me to work with a new set of colleagues, work for a new boss, build a business and try to think
through what should that portfolio look like based on my experience prior to teachers in the energy
space. We were successful in growing the private part of that program to a level on the back of
some other organizational changes in terms of trying to streamline the number of programs or
places where private investing was being undertaken. They moved myself and several colleagues into a
renamed group called Infrastructure and Natural Resources. I had day-to-day responsibilities
for Natural Resources, got familiarity with the infra team, those assets and how those contribute
to the overall portfolio. In 2018, when the previous head of capital markets had been promoted to
become the CIO, he asked me to come over and help him set up a new team called Total Fund Management,
which has become known as this TPA concept. The thoughts around that TFM group were to combine
our asset allocation function with our treasury function. I always try to explain asset allocation
is what you want to buy, treasury is how do you pay for it. That was a great combination of my public
market experience combined with my private market experience. One of the learnings that I've had
over the course of my career is that public and private, notwithstanding that those two
groups of market participants from time to time are different religions, don't like each other or
like to debate and throw rocks at each other, they're tools to implement an overall policy view
or a portfolio view. Fast forward a couple of years, the CIO resigned. Organizationally, we took
the time to think about what the right structure going forward was going to be. We arrived at a
dual CIO or a co-CIO model. I'm one of the CIOs. We've divided the responsibilities between asset
allocation and my colleague, Jillian Brown, who is the CIO of public and private investing, is
responsible for those active programs. Tim, why don't we take a step back and have you share the
history of teachers? We were established in our current format in 1990. The origin story is that
in the 1980s, the teachers union and the province of Ontario, our joint sponsors, were getting
worried about the long-term sustainability of the plan. There was a number of different commissions
and studies undertaken. They arrived at creating an independent organization called the Ontario
Teachers Pension Plan Board. A couple of key things that were important at the outset were
independence, top-notch governance. The other requirement was to make sure that we were run
as a business and had that mindset of running a world-class asset manager. The first thing
that the board did was hired our founding CEO, Claude Lamarou. One of the first things Claude
did was hire our founding CIO, Bob Bertram. Concurrent with that, the plan was seeded with
a portfolio of non-marketable province of Ontario debentures. One of the first things Bob and Claude
did, which was pretty innovative at the time, was use financial engineering, a derivative program
to transform those non-marketable debentures into a liquid portfolio of global public equities.
That was the first step to this journey of diversification across a number of different
asset classes. We're an early adopter of private equity, infrastructure, commodities, hedge funds.
You fast forward to where we are now 35 years later. We're a $300 billion plan. We cover the
retirement security of the 346,000 active retired teachers in the province. We've got a global
footprint with offices in North America, in Europe, and in Asia. We've got a real track record of
direct internal deployment of asset management. That's resulted in a funding ratio of 111%,
which goes to the long-term sustainability of the plan.
Through that entire experience, public markets, private markets, TFM, now you sit today as Co-CIO.
How do you lay out the current strategy at OTPP?
Ultimately, we're trying to build a diversify portfolio that's going to be resilient across
a number of different economic environments to make sure that we're in a position to honor
that pension promise. I would divide that investment strategy along a couple of different
dimensions, one of which would be diversification. One would be we are believers in active management.
Where and how do you focus your activities to deliver on that excess return?
Another one would be we're focused on ensuring we've got the right risk management framework in
place to deliver on that goal. The fourth one is we do use a prudent amount of leverage to
execute our investment plan. Those will be the four buckets.
How do you think about the implementation of TPA or TFM?
It's ultimately about delivering the best risk-adjusted portfolio with all the tools that
you have at your disposal. I suppose our form of that, we probably started with a type of TPA
back in 2015 or 2016 when we went down the path of a one-teacher strategy where our board before
that would say, okay, management, what is the desired asset mix? Management would present to
the board. The board would say, okay, great, that's the right asset mix. Management would then go off,
try to build a portfolio to beat that asset mix. That asset mix had some characteristics of that
risk portfolio. One of the challenges with that is making sure there's alignment with what you're
actually trying to do. Pensions are paid with total return, not with active return or just
beta return. How do you make sure that you're in a situation where everybody's aligned to deliver
the best total return on a risk-adjusted basis? As we're going through that one-teacher strategy,
the board said, hey, look, we're signing off on this asset mix, but it's what you folks are
recommending to us. Why are we taking responsibility for that? Is there a way for you folks to be
responsible for the asset mix as much as we are? That moved us down this path of having much more
flexible asset mix bands. The flip side to that is that that does not mean that you don't have a
rigorous risk approach, which we do have. To me, a reference portfolio is more of a signal of
risk appetite, not necessarily meant to give you a rigid portfolio construction exercise.
I always say, if you're going to tell me what the right risk appetite is, tell me that directly.
Then it's on management and the investment team to deliver the best risk-adjusted return
to achieve that consistent with all the guardrails that you would have from a risk perspective.
Some of the downsides of having a reference portfolio is that over time, investment teams
will gravitate to what those weights are. You can end up in a circumstance where, if for instance,
your reference portfolio is 60% equities, 40% fixed income, investment teams will be reluctant to
deviate substantially away from those weights. You can be in the world where you have a lot of fixed
income exposure, like we saw in 2020-2021, where the reason for having that in the portfolio may
not be as compelling as what it once was. You end up in a circumstance where investment teams are
reluctant to deviate even though they know that they should be deviating.
How do you bring it all together? Total fund management is focused on that top-down
asset allocation function. How do you then layer in some of that bottom-up thinking?
That's where the real magic happens from an excess return perspective.
The top-down is more my domain. My colleague, Jillian, would be responsible for that bottom-up
piece. Top-down, some of the levers would be, what is your active versus passive mix?
What is your leverage and liquidity formulation to implement that overall asset mix? The big thing
that the team spends a lot of time on is where and how do you want to position the portfolio from
a broader risk perspective? You can be complicated and we have a lot of different systems that go
into that. Our simple way to think about it is, do we want the portfolio to be positioned
aggressively, neutral or conservatively, depending on the market environment, overlaying what our
risk return BOIs are to satisfy our actuarial objectives? We're a pension plant. We have
fairly good line of sight in terms of what our liability profile is, not standing that that can
be out 60, 70, 80 years. As you look today, that high level, do you want to be aggressive, neutral,
or conservative? How do you go about making that assessment? We have a couple of different
planning horizons and investment committees to do that. The first is our planning investment process,
which is typical of the industry, but we do run an annual investment plan where we try to think
about where we want the portfolio to be over a one-year horizon. We also think about the
planning process over a five-year horizon. Five years, there's nothing magic about that. It's
far enough in the future where you don't have to do anything immediately today, but it's near
enough that you have to start taking action today if you want to accomplish it. The five-year
horizon is driven by the fact that we do have a portion of the portfolio that's in illiquid assets.
We need to make sure that we've got the right buffer to be able to manage that because you never
want to be in a position where you're a forced seller of an asset. That's why we spend a lot of
time on planning out where do we think those allocations should go. We also overlay that with
a rigorous liquidity and leverage system that's run by our risk team. That process of the one-year
horizon, which is probably more relevant for risk positioning, is the beginnings of how we want
to structure the portfolio. A one-year horizon is still an eternity in the investment business.
Within our total fund management team, there is a function which looks at more dynamic
type of opportunities, how the market might be evolving, how does that compare to our original
assumptions. The point of TFM isn't to be day trading the portfolio. These are big decisions.
We have a group that has a specific mandate within our capital markets team, which would be
frequent in nature. The TFM team and this dynamic team is there to say, look, here's what we think
the environment is. Here's what we think is currently priced in or not priced into the market.
How should we think about a portfolio adjustment driven by a couple of things? One would be
risk mitigation type of approach. If there is a particular event on the horizon
that if it were to happen would be unacceptable from a return or catastrophic loss perspective,
we probably would want to be thinking about that. The prototypical example of that would be
going into Brexit 10 years ago. If you have a large portfolio of UK or pound-based exposure
and you don't know what's going to happen, you might want to be thinking about
aggressively trying to manage some of those risks. The other example would be we have an
allocation in the portfolio. Markets have moved. Is it still going to perform its role in the
portfolio given the repricing that's happened? An example of that would have been in 2022 with
fixed income. We had an allocation to fixed income where adherence to that all-weather
philosophy. When yields continue to go lower and lower, down to almost zero, we did a lot of analysis
and our CIO at the time working with our CEO and the board said our expected return for fixed income
is low because yields were close to zero. I totally understand that yields could go negative as they
had done and were doing in Europe. Our view is that is less likely to happen in North America
given some of the commentary from central banks and other authorities. Fixed incomes roll in the
portfolio to be a offset or ballast to an equity shock is going to be more difficult. Why do we
have this in the portfolio? There was a conscious decision to reduce our fixed income exposure
that would have been driven in combination and discussion and research from that TFM group.
I'd love you to take us underneath the last time you went through your annual process,
where you came out on the five-year and the one-year thoughts.
We've spent a lot of time thinking about where do we need to focus our active activities. A typical
example of that would be what are the prospective returns for private equity? Some of our peers
in the US, for instance, have been aggressive in reducing what they would view as the expected
return for those assets. We would take the view that it has become more competitive for private
equity in terms of prospective returns. If you used to be earning five or six hundred basis
points over whatever your comparator is, if it's less than that, then you probably want to think
about what the implications are for the portfolio over that five-year time horizon. You'd never
want to be in a position where you close a door. If market conditions change, there is a case to
be made that those market conditions are changing, that you're not in a position to deploy because we
do use partners. We also have a team of internal investors that can also execute managing that
aspect of things as a pretty important part of the puzzle. When you want to flex down a little
bit private equity in that scenario, how do you do it? You need to start thinking about where do
you want it to be? How do you think about the team in place? Sometimes you need to have the
forbearance to be able to not do something rash or erratic. We do have the benefit of being fully
funded and having a flexible liquidity pool. We're never in a position where we need to
get a number to a certain level. We've taken the approach that we should be looking at opportunities
to reduce that when we think that the market or the pricing for those assets is attractive and is
still consistent with our long-term return assumptions, but not unduly force that allocation
more. In a scenario like this that you did think over five years, you might want to reduce relative
to where you were, how do you toggle the external relationships versus the internal capabilities?
Part of this is reduction of the size of that program in dollar amounts. It's probably not as
pronounced as what you would think because the fund is going to continue to grow. The asset allocation
function tries to allocate on a percent basis because we're trying to scale up and down the
overall portfolio. If you're a practitioner or a GP or an internal investor, you're also focused on
how many dollars do I have. We actually haven't seen a substantial reduction in the dollar amount
because as we forecast out these things, that acts as a bit of an offset to this percent reduction.
As you went from your five-year view to the one-year view, what were the things you were
looking at changing? More recently, there's been a lot of discussion around our inflation-sensitive
asset class, which is different than maybe some of our peers. We are an adherent to this fall
weather building a resilient portfolio. Our inflation-sensitive asset class, which we have
about 20% of our portfolio in right now, is there for two purposes. One is to provide a reasonable
return in most environments in an inflation spike or an inflationary environment, which has
historically in our estimation going forward is going to have a pretty bad impact on equity and
bond portfolios. In those types of instances, our inflation-sensitive asset class is there to provide
offsets to what we expect to be happening in our equity market. We have a couple of levers within
that basket. Our inflation-sensitive would be our public commodities, which would include gold.
We have the private natural resource team, which I grew up in in the organization. It also contains
a bucket of public market inflation-related product to give us that protection. We've spent a lot of
time. What is that inflation environment going to look like? How do we need to position that part
of the portfolio in a world that we would expect inflation to be more volatile and likely to run
at a higher weight? The other one is on the equity basket in terms of how do you think about your
equity composition? We've got private equity. We've got a venture group. We've got a public or
a passive completion part of the portfolio. Across each of those dimensions, there's positives and
negatives. On the passive side, the US concentration is something that we're trying to be thoughtful
around in terms of how do you manage that. The reality is the US is still a pretty important
market. If you want to have exposure to that AI or that technology growth theme,
it's difficult to find it in other markets. We spend a lot of time thinking about some of
those issues below the surface. When you look at that one factor of AI and growth through a lens
of risk, there's a lot of discussion of potential binary outcomes where this keeps going or maybe
something changes significantly. How do you incorporate that into your thinking about risk
in the portfolio? AI is changing so quickly that having a high conviction view is difficult.
We try to be humble. There's certain things that we don't know. You can debate whether
other people know, but we want to be balanced and not be overconfident in our ability to predict
what or how that AI theme is going to evolve. The other part of it is we want to make sure that
we're looking at the portfolio from this all-weather perspective and that we're not overbatting on a
particular outcome as it relates to AI. It's even more important given the range of outcomes associated
with it to be thinking about this portfolio resilience, recognizing that there's upside
associated with that. There's also potential downside to what happens if AI tips over to the
extent that AI ends up being a positive productivity shock historically has benefited the equity part
of the capital structure. What are some of the more recent dynamic shifts you made in that
within a year bucket presumably on the liquid side? I alluded to some of the work that we've been
doing on the inflation sensitive. There's been a lot of volatility in commodity markets. We've
used that as an opportunity where appropriate linked the impact on other asset classes. If there's
an inflation shock, how much of that inflation shock have you already captured? How do you think
about liquidity? You mentioned using some leverage. Those two things can go together.
I would separate that into the triangle of leveraged liquidity and funding that's managed by
our treasury team. Our risk team also helps us manage that part of the portfolio. Leverage and
liquidity are important because what's going to get any investor into trouble and by trouble I mean
get pushed out of a conviction view around where they think the portfolio should be structured
would be one you have a liquidity event. You can't satisfy your near term obligations. Two is
you lose a lot of money. The third is that you do things that your stakeholders aren't fans of.
On the liquidity side, it's especially important given that we do use derivatives to complete the
portfolio. We do have a rigorous process around scenario analysis and downside circumstances
to ensure that we always have substantial liquidity. That's a board limit for us. We do spend a lot of
time monitoring that. There's been a number of instances both in the U.S. with some of the
endowments going through the GFC as well as even in the Canadian pension space where some of this
leverage items that didn't have a comprehensive liquidity management profile around it got some
institutions into trouble where they were four sellers of assets at very inopportune time.
We certainly want to avoid that type of circumstance. We're going to take a quick
break in the action to tell you about Brookfield. Brookfield invests in the thing behind the thing
behind the next big thing. Their focus across infrastructure, energy, real estate, private
equity and credit is helping to build the backbone of the global economy. Brookfield combines deep
operational expertise with disciplined long-term investing, uncovering value and partnering
alongside clients to shape tomorrow's economy today. Invest in the businesses that shape tomorrow.
Learn how you can own what's next at Brookfield.com slash own.
This is not an offer to sell or investment advice. Investing involves risk,
including the loss of capital. And now, back to the show.
What type of metrics do you use to calibrate the appropriate amount of liquidity?
We would use a LCR liquidity coverage ratio type of metric. It's not quite the same as what you
would see with a bank or with a deposit taking institution because our liability structure is
substantially different than a deposit based one would be akin to an LCR type of ratio
customized for a pension plan. What's comfortable for you?
Comfortable for me is to be able to absorb a pretty substantial shock and not get pushed out of a
position. It depends on what the size of the portfolio is. It has implications with currency
hedging. A non-US based investor has a slightly different challenge with currencies where you're
tending to hedge a illiquid long dated asset with a liquid security. You do have a maturity
term mismatch. What tends to happen in a market shock is that the US dollar strengthens in this
case versus the Canadian dollar. If you've done any hedging, you tend to have to post collateral
against that. That would be one of the liquidity draws that would be factored into our LCR framework.
Have you thought about where to implement active management? Where did just gain passive exposure?
It comes down to where do you think you have an edge? That can be done both internally and
externally. It's broader than you should just do infrastructure with external managers or
internal managers. It comes down to what are the necessary ingredients for a particular strategy
to be able to deliver an excess return? What were the drivers historically? What do you think
those drivers are going to be going forward? That active versus passive discussion, which is more
of a top-down decision, paired with the bottom-up where the bottom-up deal teams will then have to
say, this is where we're going to focus our activities to achieve those types of outcomes.
Did you look across your asset classes? Where have you decided to use active versus passive on
one lens and then internal versus external on another if you're filling in that two by two?
In the equity space, passive equity versus an active public equity program has been much more
challenging, at least for us. We have scale back that program. We do have a team that still does
some active stockpicking. It's smaller than what it was a couple of years ago, given the fact that
that's a difficult and competitive market. As we look at other asset classes, private equity,
infrastructure and real estate being the big three, as well as venture. Venture introduces a
different layer of complexity to the extent that those opportunities are successful. Using a hybrid
model of external and internal, depending on where the market is and where we think we have
competitive advantage to be able to deliver on that excess return, trying to be thoughtful around
where we focus our internal resources. Where do we need to recognize that it's a activity that
we're best served by going with an external partner? How do you think about the use of hedge
funds in your portfolio? Hedge funds from a top-down perspective would fall into what we call
our absolute return strategies. The theoretical piece of that is have a high expected return
with low correlation to some of the other major factors we have, the equity and bonds.
Those are difficult to find. When you can find them, you need to be thoughtful around
how are you considering the fee component of things. We do use hedge funds in that particular
capacity to generate those non-correlated returns. In certain instances, if there's a certain skill
set or a certain type of return stream that those individuals can deliver that we just won't be able
to do internally, we are open to using that as a lever to implement our asset mix.
How have you thought about the internal use of hedge funds?
We'd have a capital markets team and they would be engaged in hedge fund-like strategies. One example
is that we do have a quantitative systematic research team. They would be using some of the
similar techniques that you would see with some of the big-name hedge funds, but they would be
doing that internally. You mentioned the venture and growth. How do you go about implementing that?
Our venture team, Teachers Venture Growth, was established in 2019. It had the role in the
portfolio at the time of giving us exposure to innovative companies that were not necessarily
available in the public market space. That team has done a fantastic job. One of the milestones
for a venture company is when they go public, I would argue a venture company going public is
a feature, not a bug. From a portfolio perspective, it does introduce this tension between private
and public investing. It's not to say that those instances didn't happen in the past with our
private equity or our INR team. It wasn't as big an issue. We're trying to be practical between
dealing with the mindset differences between a private and public investor with the fact that
the TVG team would have the most familiarity and knowledge of those particular entities.
As those now IPO companies become more mature, you need to start thinking about how do you best
position them. For the time being, we've made the determination that we want to keep the people with
the best information closest to that asset for those individuals to be the most accountable with it.
How have you thought about the position size of something as we get some of these large-scale
IPOs that you didn't have control over and now you do?
These are world-class problems when you have an asset that has become a 10, 20, 30, 40 bagger.
It's a different form of problem in terms of having a concentration risk that you've grown into,
